# Judith Chapter 10 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Codex Vaticanus, Judith 10

---

## Council Notes

**Key decisions for this chapter:**

**The cosmetic scene (vv. 2-4):** This passage is deliberate in its inventory of adornment. The Greek text enumerates each item as a form of arming. PNEUMA explicitly names Judith's beauty as a "weapon" — this is interpretively true to the narrative but the word "weapon" is not in the Greek. SOPHIA follows LOGOS's enumeration faithfully while allowing PNEUMA's insight to inform the SOPHIA council notes without inserting it into the translation text itself.

**v. 4 — "for-the-purpose-of deceiving the eyes":** The Greek *pros apatēn opthalmōn* is unambiguous: to deceive eyes. All three translators note the deliberateness. EMET: "for-the-purpose-of deceiving the eyes." LOGOS: "in order to beguile the eyes." PNEUMA: "to catch the eye." SOPHIA: "to deceive the eyes" — the Greek says *apatān* (deception), not mere attraction.

**v. 10 — "fell upon her face" — the final verse:** The men of the city watch Judith depart. PNEUMA adds narrative color but SOPHIA stays with LOGOS's economy.

**v. 14 — "wonderfully beautiful" / "strikingly beautiful":** EMET's "wonderfully-beautiful" (*kalē sphodra*) is the most literal. LOGOS: "strikingly beautiful." PNEUMA: "stunning." SOPHIA: "exceedingly beautiful" — closest to the Greek adverb *sphodra*.

**v. 19 — "who can despise this people?":** The soldiers' reaction is crucial. They do not admire Judith alone — they recalibrate their assessment of Israel because of her. PNEUMA captures this energy well. LOGOS is more measured. SOPHIA follows LOGOS structurally but allows "Who could despise a people" which is more rhetorical.

**v. 22 — "silver lamps going before him":** EMET: "silver lamps were-going-before him." LOGOS: "with silver lamps carried before him." PNEUMA: "silver lamps blazing ahead of him." SOPHIA: "silver lamps were carried before him" — ceremonial procession, not "blazing."

**v. 23 — "the beauty of her face" stunned the room:** PNEUMA's "sheer beauty of it was a blow" is vivid. SOPHIA notes this as PNEUMA's best moment in the chapter but does not adopt the violence metaphor. LOGOS's "they all marveled at the beauty of her face" is the SOPHIA ruling.

---

**10:1** When Judith had finished crying out to the God of Israel and had completed all these words,

**10:2** she rose from where she lay on her face and called her maidservant and went down into the house. She took off the sackcloth and removed her widow's clothing.

**10:3** She bathed her body with water, anointed herself with rich myrrh, dressed her hair, set a tiara on her head, and put on the festive garments she had worn during the lifetime of her husband Manasseh.

**10:4** She put sandals on her feet and put on her ankle-rings, bracelets, rings, earrings, and all her adornments, making herself as beautiful as could be — in order to deceive the eyes of whatever men might see her.

**10:5** She gave her maidservant a skin of wine and a flask of oil, filled a pouch with roasted grain, cakes of dried figs, and fine bread, wrapped all her provisions together, and placed them on her maidservant.

**10:6** They went out to the gate of the city of Bethulia and found Uzziah standing there with the city elders, Chabris and Charmis.

**10:7** When they saw her — her face transformed and her clothing changed — they were utterly astonished at her beauty and said to her:

**10:8** "May the God of our ancestors grant you favor and accomplish your purpose, for the glory of the children of Israel and the exaltation of Jerusalem." And she bowed in worship before God.

**10:9** She said to them, "Order them to open the city gate for me." They ordered the young men to open it, as she had asked.

**10:10** They did so. Judith went out, she and her maidservant with her. The men of the city watched her until she had descended the mountain and passed through the valley, and they could see her no longer.

**10:11** As they were going through the valley, an Assyrian patrol encountered them.

**10:12** They seized her and demanded, "What people do you belong to? Where have you come from, and where are you going?" She replied, "I am a daughter of the Hebrews, and I am fleeing from before them, for they are about to be handed over to you as plunder.

**10:13** I am on my way to Holofernes, the commander-in-chief of your army, to report truthful intelligence. I will show him the route by which he can advance and take the entire hill country without losing a single man or a single life from his forces."

**10:14** When the men heard her words and looked upon her face — for she was exceedingly beautiful in their sight — they said to her:

**10:15** "You have saved your life by hurrying down to present yourself to our lord. And now, come to his tent. Some of us will escort you until we hand you over to him.

**10:16** When you stand before him, do not be afraid — tell him what you have told us, and he will treat you well."

**10:17** They selected a hundred men from their company, assigned them to escort her and her maidservant, and brought them to the tent of Holofernes.

**10:18** A commotion spread throughout the entire camp, for the news of her arrival was announced from tent to tent. They came out and gathered around her as she stood outside the tent of Holofernes while they were announcing her.

**10:19** They were astonished at her beauty and were filled with wonder at the Israelites because of her, each man saying to his neighbor, "Who could despise a people that has women like this among them? It is not wise to leave a single man among them alive — for those who were let go could deceive the whole earth."

**10:20** Those who slept beside Holofernes and all his attendants came out and led her into the tent.

**10:21** Holofernes was resting on his bed beneath a canopy woven of purple and gold, set with emeralds and precious stones.

**10:22** They announced her to him and he came out into the anteroom, with silver lamps carried before him.

**10:23** When Judith came before him and before his attendants, they all marveled at the beauty of her face. She fell down before him on her face, and his servants raised her up.
